items.desc: The Philly duo’s folk music radiates a special kind of energy. Their second album is tinged with psychedelia, a wicker wunderkammer of songs, spells, and secrets.
items.title: Autosmile

items.desc: Torn between Texas and Topanga but fully herself, the songwriter sounds at home in the outlaw country idiom on an intimate, searching new record produced by Shooter Jennings.
items.title: A Mile South of Heaven

items.desc: Modeled after the literary concept of the hero’s journey, the Catalan composer’s latest album is her most ambitious yet: It’s weirder, wilder, and more dazzling than anything she’s done to date.
items.title: Dja Dja

items.desc: With new songs that rank among his very best, the Geese frontman’s solo live album is an exquisite rendering of a had-to-be-there night and a work of real-time mythmaking.
items.title: Live at Carnegie Hall

items.desc: The UK artist brings a frenzy of club-grime provocation and internet humor to his glitched-out emo, but his portrayal of small-town malaise is what makes it a riot.
items.title: THIS IS SPA TOWN!

items.desc: Tinashe’s eighth album is her best and bravest yet: more ambitious, more focused, and effortlessly in touch with the zeitgeist. It’s the best pop album of the year.
items.title: Popstar

items.desc: Exploding its signature blend of noise-punk and dance music to masterful extremes, the Irish band gets louder, rawer, funnier, and more methodical on its exhilarating fourth album.
items.title: Pugnello

items.desc: Earnest and disaffected, ironic and confrontational, the Brooklyn songwriter’s Sub Pop debut channels trans rage into scrappy DIY punk with no patience left.
items.title: Ultimate Love Forever

items.desc: Kurt Wagner reinvents his band yet again, this time slimming down to a bare-bones acoustic setup and stripping away the studio artifice. But his storytelling remains as expansive as ever.
items.title: Punching the Clown

items.desc: The experimental Brooklyn project returns with a serene and spectral new album, using an ever-shifting musical backdrop to explore themes of illusion and doubt.
items.title: fata morgana

items.desc: For her third solo album, Phoebe Bridgers expands and contracts, capturing experiences that are strange, solitary, and hers alone. It is the quietest, most cohesive record in her discography.
items.title: Lost Weekend

items.desc: There are many rappers out there who dig deep into their lives for heavy stories of pain and sorrow. The DMV rapper does this too, but he elevates the art form to a whole new level.
items.title: Somewhere Over the Rainbow

items.desc: Natal Zaks brings dub techno to a higher level on an energetic and atmospheric 2x12", another pin in the lapel of the new and outstanding Short Span label.
items.title: Uuuuuuuu

items.desc: On the follow-up to BRAT, the pop auteur pivots to a referential, proudly tossed-off rock sound that offers mystifying glances behind the curtain of stardom.
items.title: Music, Fashion, Film

items.desc: The longtime Arthur Russell collaborator finally gets a solo exhibition: a gorgeously realized and fundamentally incomplete work of sensual art-folk, leftfield disco, and experimental synth-pop. It’s at once an archival triumph and one of the year’s most thrilling new releases.
items.title: My Skyscraper

items.desc: The L.A. improv quintet made its first two LPs by remixing key moments from its gigs; now, on a pair of astonishing unedited live takes, the group proves that performance is the heart of its music.
items.title: Spontaneous Music Live

items.desc: The pop star’s third album is a heartbreaking account of an intense romance and its demise. Its mood is perfectly reflected in the music, and her evolution as a songwriter is a sight to behold.
items.title: you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love

items.desc: The Miami duo’s electrifying, boundary-bending combination of Haitian kompa, underground rap, reggaeton, electro-pop, and baile funk is loud as hell and rich in egalitarian spirit.
items.title: EXIT 2B

items.desc: Laced with occult imagery and enigmatic samples, the Scottish duo’s immersive new album—their first in 13 years—offers some of the most captivating music of their career.
items.title: Inferno

items.desc: On her spellbinding fifth album, Aldous Harding steps closer than ever to the camera lens without coming into focus. It’s an oblique character study of herself, and the best album of her career so far.
items.title: Train on the Island

items.desc: The ambient musician’s new album is a tremendous leap in scale, a quiet conjuring of vast, prayerlike yearning.
items.title: Poem 1

items.desc: Retro but never dusty, the rapper’s brilliantly bugged-out new tape sounds like a New York that hardly exists anymore.
items.title: LIVING TYPE DANGEROUS Vol. 1

items.desc: Former Black Midi bassist Cameron Picton’s dazzlingly complicated solo debut is a tangle of baroque melodies, chamber-punk arrangements, and garden-path lyrics.
items.title: My New Band Believe

items.desc: On a daring new album, the singer-songwriter and guitar virtuoso examines happiness, love, and memory with a forensic curiosity.
items.title: Wendy Eisenberg

items.desc: Smelling like burnt rubber and mall body mist, the pop provocateur’s loud, wild new album swerves hard into club antagonism.
items.title: WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA
